opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'm pretty skeptical, to be honest. I think VLAs are a useful engineering hack for the short term, but I don't think they're the path to really capable robots.

The basic idea is to take a large language model, or a vision-language model, bolt an action head on it, and fine-tune it on a bunch of robot demonstrations. And you get something that can do some tasks, sometimes reasonably well, in situations that look like the training data. But fundamentally it's still the same paradigm: a reactive system that maps observations to actions. There's no real understanding of the physical world in there, no ability to predict the consequences of its actions, and therefore no ability to plan.

The problem is that language is not where the knowledge about the physical world lives. A four-year-old has seen more data through vision than the biggest LLMs have been trained on in text. Most of what we know about how the world works, that objects fall, that you can push something but not pull it with a rope the wrong way, all that intuitive physics, is not in text. So starting from a language model and hoping it somehow figures out how to manipulate objects is, I think, going about it backwards.

And then there's the data issue. Robot demonstration data is expensive and scarce. You're never going to collect enough teleoperation data to cover all the situations a robot will encounter in the real world. That's why we have robots that can do impressive demos, but we still don't have a domestic robot that can clear the dinner table and load the dishwasher, something any ten-year-old learns in one shot.

What I think we need instead are world models: systems that learn, mostly from video and observation, abstract representations of how the world evolves, and can predict what will happen if they take a given action. That's what we've been working on with JEPA architectures, joint embedding predictive architectures, where you predict in representation space rather than trying to predict every pixel. Once you have a good world model, you can do planning: you search for a sequence of actions that optimizes an objective, subject to constraints, guardrails. That's objective-driven AI. It's much more like how humans and animals actually operate, and it requires much less task-specific data, because the bulk of the learning is self-supervised.

So, VLAs: fine for now, people will get some products out of them. But in a few years, I think most people will have moved toward world-model-based planning, and VLAs will look like a transitional phase.

r001.rationale: The candidate expresses personal skepticism and calls VLAs a short-term engineering hack, but says they can perform some tasks and yield products. It does not say the approach is now generally regarded as failing.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I'm going to be the skeptic here, as usual. VLA models are a reasonable thing to do right now because they work to some extent, and they let people build demos. You take a large pretrained vision-language model, you bolt on an action head, you fine-tune on teleoperation data, and the robot can fold a towel or pick up a cup when you ask it in English. That's impressive relative to where we were five years ago. But I don't think this is the path to robots that are actually useful, that can learn a new task in a few trials, and that you can trust in a kitchen with your kids.

The fundamental problem is the same one I have with LLMs. These systems are essentially trained to predict the next action, or the next chunk of actions, conditioned on pixels and text. Autoregressive prediction of discrete tokens is fine for language because language is discrete and low-bandwidth. The physical world is continuous, high-dimensional, and mostly unpredictable at the level of pixels. If you train a system to predict exactly what's going to happen in the world, you waste all your capacity on details that are irrelevant. And if you ask it to predict actions directly from observations, you get something that imitates, but doesn't understand. It doesn't have a model of the world. It has a very large lookup table with interpolation.

And data is the killer. Language models work because there's trillions of tokens of text lying around. There is no equivalent for robot actions. Every lab is collecting teleop data with a few hundred people wearing gloves or driving arms, and it's tiny compared to what the internet gives you for text. So people say, "We'll use the language model to transfer knowledge." Sure, the language part gives you some semantic grounding, you can say "the red cup" and it knows what red and cup are. But that doesn't give the system any intuition about physics, about how objects behave when you push them, about contact dynamics. A cat has that, and a cat has no language whatsoever.

What I think we need instead is systems that learn world models from observation, in a self-supervised way, in abstract representation space. Not predicting pixels, predicting representations, which is what we've been doing with JEPA. Then you plan. You have an objective, you have a model that tells you what state you'll end up in if you take this sequence of actions, and you optimize the actions to minimize cost. That's model-predictive control, which is old, but with learned models. That gives you systems that can do things they've never been trained to do, because they can reason about consequences. A VLA cannot do that. If the situation isn't in the training distribution, it just produces something plausible-looking, and plausible-looking is dangerous when there's a hundred-kilogram robot involved.

So my assessment is that VLAs are a useful stepping stone and a decent engineering product for the next couple of years. People will build companies on them, and some tasks will get done. But as a research direction toward real embodied intelligence, I think it's a bit of a dead end, in the same way that I think scaling autoregressive LLMs is a dead end toward human-level intelligence. We're going to have to go back and solve the problem of learning world models from sensory data, and I'd rather we spent the effort there.

r001.rationale: The response calls VLAs useful now and a decent near-term engineering product. It argues they are a dead end as a research direction, but does not say they are generally regarded as failing.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re an interesting approach, but I don’t think they’re sufficient by themselves. You can use a vision-language model to interpret an instruction and identify things in a scene, and then train it to produce actions from demonstrations. That can give you useful behavior. The question is how well that behavior generalizes when the robot encounters a situation that wasn’t represented in its training data.

What’s missing, in my view, is a world model: a model that allows the system to predict the consequences of its actions. If I move this object, what happens? If I try to grasp it this way, will it slip? You want the robot to be able to consider possible actions, predict their outcomes, and choose a sequence that accomplishes its objective.

And that prediction doesn’t have to happen in language, or even at the level of pixels. It should happen in a representation that captures the aspects of the world that matter for the task and leaves out irrelevant details.

So I see a role for vision-language-action models within a larger architecture. But I’m skeptical that simply scaling up imitation learning on robot trajectories will give us the kind of flexible, common-sense physical intelligence we want.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls vision-language-action models an interesting approach and says they are insufficient by themselves; it does not characterize them as an approach now generally regarded as failing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re an interesting approach, but I don’t think they’re sufficient to get us to general-purpose robots. You can train a system to map images and language instructions into actions, and it can learn useful behaviors from demonstrations. The difficulty is what happens when it encounters a situation that’s different from the training data.

What’s missing is a world model: a system that can predict the consequences of actions. If a robot wants to move an object, it should be able to anticipate what will happen if it pushes here or grasps there, and then plan a sequence of actions to achieve its objective. It shouldn’t have to discover every possible solution through demonstrations or trial and error.

And that prediction doesn’t need to happen at the pixel level. You want to predict in an abstract representation that captures the relevant properties of the world and leaves out details that are unpredictable or irrelevant to the task.

So vision-language-action models can be useful components. But I would put them in a larger architecture with a learned world model, objectives, and planning. Learning a policy directly is useful; having the ability to reason about the consequences of your actions is what makes that policy adaptable.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls vision-language-action models useful but insufficient on their own for general-purpose robots. It does not characterize them as an approach generally regarded as failing.
